title: Paramedic urges use of quicker tranquillizer
article: --- A Regina paramedic whose patient died after being pepper sprayed and sedated says he wishes he could have used a quicker, "safer," tranquillizing drug -- like paramedics have access to in Alberta.
"We feel these tools would be better utilized in the field than what we currently use," Jason Williams testified Wednesday at the third day of an inquest into the death of Vernon Dale Crowe.

The 32-year-old Regina man died on July 10, 2001 just 20 minutes after willingly climbing into an ambulance following an epileptic seizure. The six-person jury isn't allowed to assess blame, but can make recommendations to prevent similar deaths.

Asked by coroner Hugh Harradence if he had any recommendations to suggest, Williams said Saskatchewan paramedics' "tools in the tool box" don't necessarily meet the needs on the street. As a result, they often have to rely on police to assist in restraining an aggressive patient.
Williams called three times for police after Crowe abruptly went from compliant to combative. "He was a very nice guy -- then suddenly changed," he said.

When Const. Dean Ross arrived and suggested pepper spraying Crowe, Williams said he just wanted Crowe handcuffed so he could sedate him. But after Crowe twice bit the officer and once head- butted him, neither Williams nor his partner objected to Ross spraying Crowe.
"I felt the situation was escalating beyond my control ... I deferred to his (the officer's) experience," Williams said.

Immediately afterwards, Williams injected Crowe with Halidol, but the sedative isn't effective for 10 to 12 minutes. Williams said in Alberta -- where he's also licensed -- paramedics can use Versed, a quicker-acting tranquillizer that is three to four times more potent than Valium.

Williams called it a "safer" drug than Halidol, especially when a patient's medical history is unknown or the person has suffered a seizure or heart attack. It would have been his drug of choice in Crowe's case, but Saskatchewan paramedics aren't allowed to administer Versed, he testified.
While admitting Versed has its own problematic side-effects, such as breathing difficulties, Williams said paramedics are well- equipped to handle them.

A pathologist is expected to testify Crowe died of "excited delirium." Asked if paramedics should be trained about the condition -- which wasn't explained to the jury -- Williams replied, "that's a term that's just become popular." He said he's seen videos on excited delirium since Crowe's death, but paramedics have always been taught to monitor a person's breathing.

Although Crowe was placed on his stomach after he was sedated and pepper sprayed, his face was turned sideways, Williams said. When paramedics became concerned about his breathing and turned him on his back, they realized he had vomited, the inquest heard. Once Crowe was on his back, Williams learned his patient had no heartbeat.
Williams said his only other recommendation would be for direction on how to deal with people who appear to need help, but don't want it.
Crowe's cousin earlier testified that Crowe liked to roam about after a seizure. Williams said letting Crowe leave wasn't an option because he was a risk to himself and others.
